Diplomatic relations between the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) and the [Islamic Republic of Pakistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Republic_of_Pakistan "Islamic Republic of Pakistan") were established in 1950, when the [Dominion of Pakistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan "Dominion of Pakistan") was among the first countries to sever diplomatic relations with the [Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") (ROC) [government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_Republic_of_China "Government of the Republic of China") in favour of recognizing the PRC as the legitimate representative of China. Since then, relations between the two countries have been extremely cordial for the last few decades, which are influenced by their similar geopolitical and mutual interests. Although both countries have vast cultural and religious differences, they have developed a [special partnership](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_partnerships_of_China "Diplomatic partnerships of China"). Both countries have placed considerable importance on the maintenance of the relationship between them, and their regular exchanges of high-level visits have culminated in the establishment of various cooperative measures. China has provided economic, technical, and military assistance to Pakistan; both sides regard each other as close strategic allies. The two countries define their relationship as an [all-weather strategic cooperative partnership](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diplomatic_partnerships_of_China "List of diplomatic partnerships of China").

Bilateral relations have evolved from China's initial policy of neutrality to an extensive partnership driven primarily by Pakistan's strategic importance. The two countries formally resolved all of their boundary disputes with the [Sino-Pakistan Agreement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Pakistan_Agreement "Sino-Pakistan Agreement") of 1963, and Chinese military assistance to Pakistan began in 1966; a strategic alliance was formed in 1972, and economic cooperation had begun in earnest by 1979. Consequently, China has become Pakistan's third-largest trading partner overall. In 1986, Pakistani president [Zia-ul-Haq](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zia-ul-Haq "Zia-ul-Haq") visited China to improve diplomatic relations, and Pakistan was one of the to offer support to China in the aftermath of the [1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre"). More recently, China has moved forward with an agreement to cooperate in improving the [Pakistani civil nuclear power sector](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_in_Pakistan "Nuclear power in Pakistan"). In 2015, the two countries launched the [China–Pakistan Economic Corridor](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China–Pakistan_Economic_Corridor "China–Pakistan Economic Corridor"), which is part of the larger [Belt and Road Initiative](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_and_Road_Initiative "Belt and Road Initiative").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Pakistan_embassy_Beijing.jpg/250px-Pakistan_embassy_Beijing.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pakistan_embassy_Beijing.jpg)

Pakistan embassy in [Beijing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China.

Maintaining close relations with China is also a central part of [Pakistan's foreign policy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Pakistan "Foreign relations of Pakistan"). On the military front, the [People's Liberation Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") and the [Pakistan Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Armed_Forces "Pakistan Armed Forces") share a notably close relationship; China has supported Pakistan's position on the [Kashmir conflict](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir_conflict "Kashmir conflict"), while Pakistan has supported China's position on [Xinjiang](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"), [Tibet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_sovereignty_debate "Tibetan sovereignty debate"), the [territorial disputes in the South China Sea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_disputes_in_the_South_China_Sea "Territorial disputes in the South China Sea"), the [Sino-Indian border dispute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_border_dispute "Sino-Indian border dispute") and the [political status of Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_status_of_Taiwan "Political status of Taiwan"). Military cooperation between the two sides has continued to increase significantly, with joint projects producing armaments ranging from fighter jets to guided missile frigates. The overwhelming majority of Pakistan's arms imports are from China, and the country makes up the majority of China's arms exports. Both countries have generally pursued a bilateral policy that focuses to strengthen their alliance in all areas. While serving as China's main bridge to the [Muslim world](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world"), Pakistan has also played an important role in closing the communication gap between China and the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")—namely through the [1972 visit by Richard Nixon to China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_visit_by_Richard_Nixon_to_China "1972 visit by Richard Nixon to China"). Recent rankings have described Pakistan as the country that is most under Chinese political influence.

[![JF-17 Thunder.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Passu_Gojal_hunza_pakistan.jpg/250px-Passu_Gojal_hunza_pakistan.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Passu_Gojal_hunza_pakistan.jpg)

[Karakoram Highway](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram_Highway "Karakoram Highway") connects the two states.

Pakistan has a long and strong relationship with China. The long-standing ties between the two countries have been mutually beneficial. A close identity of views and mutual interests remain the centre-point of bilateral ties. Since the 1962 [Sino-Indian War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_War "Sino-Indian War"), Pakistan has supported China on most issues of importance to the latter, especially those related to [Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), [Xinjiang](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"), and [Tibet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet_Autonomous_Region "Tibet Autonomous Region") and other sensitive issues deemed by the West as [human rights](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") issues.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The Chinese leadership has acknowledged Pakistan's steadfast support on key issues. Pakistan helped China in reestablishing formal ties with the West, where they helped make possible the [1972 Nixon visit to China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Nixon_visit_to_China "1972 Nixon visit to China").[[2]](#cite_note-diplo2011-2) Pakistan has collaborated with China in extensive military and economic projects, seeing both as counterweights to an Indian-Western alliance. Pakistan has also served as a conduit for China's influence in the Muslim world.

China also has a consistent record of supporting Pakistan in regional issues. Pakistan's military depends heavily on [Chinese armaments](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equipment_Development_Department_of_the_Central_Military_Commission "Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission"), and joint projects of both economic and militaristic importance are ongoing. China has supplied blueprints to support Pakistan's nuclear program.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Amin argues that the basis of the Sino-Pak entente from its beginning has been "a mutual need to pool together resources to contain perceived Indian aspirations to hegemony over South Asia".[[4]](#cite_note-londonchurchillcollege.ac.uk-4) He continues: "Both China and Pakistan regard the entente as necessary to maintain a balance of power in the subcontinent favourable to themselves against an India that is believed by both Chinese and Pakistani strategists to be an expansionist power that occupies land regarded as properly belonging to Beijing and Islamabad respectively, and that is intent on expanding further".[[4]](#cite_note-londonchurchillcollege.ac.uk-4)

[CCP General Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") and [Iranian Supreme Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Leader_of_Iran "Supreme Leader of Iran") [Ali Khamenei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Khamenei "Ali Khamenei").

**China–Iran relations** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 中国–伊朗关系, [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language"): روابط ایران و چین) refer to the [bilateral relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilateralism "Bilateralism") between the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") and [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"). The relationship between the two civilizations is one of the oldest continuous contacts in history, stretching back more than 2,500 years. Their earliest interactions began when the [Achaemenid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") and the [Zhou dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty "Zhou dynasty") had indirect contact in the 6th century BC.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The first direct and official contact started between the [Parthian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthian_Empire "Parthian Empire") and [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") around 200 BC, when the Chinese envoy [Zhang Qian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qian "Zhang Qian") encountered the Parthian court.[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 115 BC, Emperor [Wu of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wu_of_Han "Emperor Wu of Han"), seeking to expand trade—especially in his search for high-quality horse herds—sent envoys with gifts to the court of [Mithridates II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mithridates_II_of_Parthia "Mithridates II of Parthia").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Zhang_Qian.jpg/250px-Zhang_Qian.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zhang_Qian.jpg)

The 138–126 BC travels of [Zhang Qian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qian "Zhang Qian") to the West, [Mogao Caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogao_Caves "Mogao Caves"), 618–712 AD [mural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural").

Persian merchants became the main carriers of goods and culture across Central Asia, bringing their religions, music, and ideas into China.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Ambassadors were exchanged, and Chinese travelers visited Iran regularly. Each side introduced new goods to the other, the most famous of which was [Chinese silk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_industry_in_China "Silk industry in China"). The trade route carrying this precious commodity from China to Europe passed through Iran, becoming known as the [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road"), with Iran controlling much of the trade that moved silk, metals, glass, and textiles between East and West.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

During the [Sassanid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire"), royal marriages took place.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Several Sassanid kings and nobles married Chinese princesses or women from influential Chinese families to strengthen ties. These unions symbolized the close relationship between the two sides. Persian communities [lived in Chinese cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranians_in_China "Iranians in China") during the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"), and after the fall of Sassanid Empire, some Sassanid princes even took refuge in China.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Trade also expanded by sea, with Persian sailors linking the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") to Chinese ports.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) In the 13th century during the [Mongol era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire"), Iran (under [Ilkhanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilkhanate "Ilkhanate")) and China (under [Yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty")) were part of a single empire.

In modern times, official diplomatic relations were established in 1937 between the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") and [Pahlavi Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pahlavi_Iran "Pahlavi Iran"). During the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") before the mid-1960s, Iran was generally aligned against the People's Republic of China until both countries' relations with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") shifted. After the [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"), China and the U.S. were both distrusted, but subsequent sanctions by the west pushed Iran closer to the east.[[11]](#cite_note-:7-11) Cooperation gradually expanded, with China purchasing more than 80 percent of [Iran's shipped oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_Iran "Energy in Iran") by 2025 and becoming a leading investor in transportation and industrial projects.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Relations deepened through long-term economic agreements and [China's Belt and Road Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_and_Road_Initiative "Belt and Road Initiative"), making Iran one of China's most important [strategic partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_partnerships_of_China "Diplomatic partnerships of China"). In 2021, the two nations signed a 25-year cooperation agreement.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

### Achaemenid-Zhou era

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China%E2%80%93Iran_relations&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Achaemenid-Zhou era")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_%28detail_3%29.jpg/330px-Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_%28detail_3%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_(detail_3).jpg)

Detail of the stone panel painting on the sarcophagus, depicting two [nimbate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimbate "Nimbate") male figures dressing in [Sasanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire")-style attire, drinking wine and playing [pipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipa "Pipa"). [Tomb of Yu Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Yu_Hong "Tomb of Yu Hong"), 6th century CE.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_%28detail_1%29.jpg/330px-Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_%28detail_1%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Painted_Panel_of_the_Sarcophagus_of_Y%C3%BC_Hung_(detail_1).jpg)

Left: a man holding a plate of fruits; right: a bearded man is performing the [Huteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huteng "Huteng") ("Barbarian leap") dance. Both figures have haloes. [Tomb of Yu Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Yu_Hong "Tomb of Yu Hong"), 6th century CE.

There were indirect contact between the two sides in 550-330 BC. The Achaemenid Empire, stretching from the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") to [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia") between the 6th and 4th centuries BC, pushed the Persian frontier close to regions that later connected directly with China. Although no formal diplomatic exchange is recorded between the two sides during this period, trade routes that would later form the Silk Road already existed in primitive form. Goods, ideas, and technologies moved step-by-step through Central Asian intermediaries, linking the two civilizations long before they physically met. Chinese texts reference Iran/Persia as *Bosi*. In essence, the relationship was not one of direct diplomacy but of early trans-Eurasian connectivity, laying the foundation for the deeper relations that would flourish later.

The [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") diplomat and explorer [Zhang Qian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Qian "Zhang Qian"), who visited neighboring [Bactria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bactria "Bactria") and [Sogdiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sogdiana "Sogdiana") in 126 BCE, made the first known Chinese report on [Parthia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthian_Empire "Parthian Empire"). In his accounts, Parthia is named "Ānxí" (Chinese: 安息), a transliteration of "[Arsacid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsacid_Empire "Arsacid Empire")", the name of the Parthian dynasty. Zhang Qian clearly identifies Parthia as an advanced urban civilization, whose development he equates to those of [Dayuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayuan "Dayuan") (in [Ferghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferghana "Ferghana")) and [Daxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daxia "Daxia") (in [Bactria](

Some of them, known as *[semu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semu "Semu")* ("assorted officials"), occupied important official posts in the Yuan state administration.[[20]](#cite_note-20) One of the most famous settlers from Bukhara was [Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sayyid_Ajjal_Shams_al-Din_Omar "Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar"), who is identified as an ancestor of many Chinese [Hui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hui_people "Hui people") lineages and that of [Yunnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunnan "Yunnan")'s [Panthay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panthay "Panthay") Hui population. His most famous descendant was [Zheng He](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_He "Zheng He"),[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] who became the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty")'s most famous explorer.

Han Chinese general Guo Baoyu campaigned with [Genghis in Central Asia against the Khwarezmian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_the_Khwarazmian_Empire "Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire"), and his grandson [Guo Kan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Kan "Guo Kan") campaigned under Hulagu at [the Nizari fortresess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_campaign_against_the_Nizaris "Mongol campaign against the Nizaris") of [Maymundiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Maymun-Diz "Siege of Maymun-Diz") and Alamut, as well as at [Baghdad in 1258](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(1258) "Siege of Baghdad (1258)") in Iraq. They were direct descendants of [Guo Ziyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Ziyi "Guo Ziyi").[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Expansion_of_the_Mongol_Empire.svg/250px-Expansion_of_the_Mongol_Empire.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Expansion_of_the_Mongol_Empire.svg)

Expansion of the [Mongol Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire") from 1206 to 1294

In the 1220s, the Mongols sent Khitan and Han Chinese administrators to Bukhara and Samarqand to govern, and this was witnessed by [Qiu Chuji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiu_Chuji "Qiu Chuji") on his way to meet Genghis Khan in Afghanistan.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Chinese siege engineers were deployed in Iran and Iraq by the Ilkhanate.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) The Khitan [Yelü Chucai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yel%C3%BC_Chucai "Yelü Chucai") was sent by the Mongols to Central Asia.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

The war between Qaidu and Kublai wrecked the economy of [Qocho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qocho "Qocho") and stopped trade between China and West Asia and Europe.[[28]](#cite_note-28) During the war between Kublai Khan and Kaidu, the Uyghurs of Qocho (Gaochang) fled Qaidu's assaults into Gansu, under Yuan control from Turfan, in 1283, placing Yongchang as their capital and between 1270 and 1275, making Gansu's city of Qamil their capital. Uyghur subjects fled along with the royal court.[[29]](#cite_note-29) The Mongols sent new people to repopulate the Jaxartes river (lower Syr Darya) and the city of Yangikent (Iamkint or Sakint) after deporting and killing the natives. The upper Yenisei region of Qianqianzhou received many Han Chinese artisans and the western Mongolia-based military base and granary city of Chinqai received many Han Chinese artisans put there by Mongols, as heard in 1221–1222 by Li Zhichang, who was going to Central Asia. Kublai Khan sent southern Han Chinese farmers from the Southern Song repeatedly to the Siberian Kyrgyz region of Yenisei in 1272, and before that year as well. He also sent them farming equipment and oxen. Tanguts, Khitans, and Han Chinese were sent to take care of gardens and fields in the depopulated and sacked city of Samarkand, where only 25% of the original 100,000 households survived the Mongol sacking, and Han Chinese artisans were "everywhere" in the ruined city, as witnessed on 3 December 1221. They managed to rehabilitate and reconstruct the city, since Samarqand was praised as a productive flourishing area before at least 1225, when the Khitan Yelu Chucai came there. Mongke sent Chang De to Hulagu in 1259. He went across Central Asia. He said, "numerous Chinese growing wheat, barley, millet, and [other] grains" lived around Lake Qizilbash and the Ulungur river in north Dzungaria and the cities of Almaliq and Tiermuer Chancha had many Han Chinese from Shaanxi in the Ili river valley. He said, "the Muslim populace [there] has become mixed with the Chinese and over time, their customs have gradually come to resemble those of the Middle Kingdom."[[30]](#cite_note-30) During Mongke's rule in the 1250s in Iran in the 13th century, Iran received thousands of Han Chinese farmers. Han Chinese were the plurality in the Iranian Azerbaijan city of Khoy as of 1340, as testified by Mustawfi. Han Chinese in Khoy and Tabriz in Iranian Azerbaijan were originally sent to Marv by the Mongols before being sent to the Iranian Azerbaijani cities, as recorded by Rashid al-Din.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Rashid al-din said that the Chinese millet grain known as tuki was brought by Han Chinese first to Marv in Turkmenistan and then to Iranian Azerbaijan in Khoy and Tabriz. Later, Han Chinese were reported to be the most significant ethnicity generations later, in Khoi around 1340, when Mustawfi wrote about them.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Rashid al-din wrote it in 1310. And local Muslims in Almalik lived with Han Chinese and Han Chinese were employed as guards and millet, barley, and wheat farmers around Beshbalik and worked in Samarkand as seen in 1259 by Liu Yu. Wheat and hemp were grown next to mud huts near the Kerulun river by Han Chinese farmers in 1247 near Karakorum, as seen by Zhang Dehui. Han Chinese made up 70% of herders in Mongolia, as seen by Xuting and Peng Daya. Siberia's Upper Yeniesei area, Samarkand, and western Mongolia all had Han Chinese craftsmen, as seen by Li Zhichang in 1221–1222. He visited Balkh, Samarkand, and Tashkent when he went to Central Asia and Mongolia from Shandong.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)

The Tabriz-based Rob'-e Rashidi and the Maraghe observatory in Ilkhanid Iran had scientists and scholars of Chinese origin. The "Book of Precious Presents or the Medicine of the Chinese People" (Tansuq-name ya tebb-e ahl-e Kheta) was translated by people working under Rashid-al-Din Fazl-Allah to Persian from Chinese and it was about [Chinese medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_medicine "Chinese medicine").[[37]](#cite_note-37)

[Rashid al-Din](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashid-al-Din_Hamadani "Rashid-al-Din Hamadani") wrote about Chinese culture and history.[[38]](#cite_note-38)[[39]](#cite_note-39) Oljeitu's birth was witnessed by Rashid al-Din.[[40]](#cite_note-40) The Sunni convert Jew Rashid al-Din was executed after the Ilkhanate became Shia.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

Han Chinese were sent to the Upper Yenisei valley as weavers, into Samarkand and Outer Mongolia as craftsmen, as noticed by Ch'ang-ch'un in 1221-22 when he travelled to Kabul from Beijing and they moved to Russia and Iran. The Euphrates and Tigris basins were irrigated by Chinese hydraulic engineers and in 1258, at the siege of Baghdad, one of Hulagu Khan's generals was Han Chinese. Because of the Mongols, Chinese influenced architecture, music, ceramics, and Persian miniatures in the Golden Horde and Il-khan. Han Chinese, Mongols, Uighurs, Venetians, and Geonese all lived in Tabriz, where paper money was introduced and movable type printing and wood engraving as well as paper money, printed fabrics, and playing cards spread from China to Europe due to the Mongols. Wood engraving which was Chinese was mentioned in the 1313 book "Treasure of the Il-khan on the Sciences of Cathay", which was about Chinese medicine and translated by Rashid al-Din.[[42]](#cite_note-42) The Mongols brought the Chinese idea of paper currency to Iran in 1294 where the name of the currency, chaw, was taken from the Chinese word Chao.[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48)[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52)

During the Mongol-Yuan period, some historians claim Persian was the *[lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca")* of [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia"), and many Persians and Central Asians migrated to China. There was a large Persian community in China, especially among Chinese Muslims, and claim that [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language") was one of the official languages of the [Yuan dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty"), alongside [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language") and [Mongolian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_language "Mongolian language").[[53]](#cite_note-:0-53) However, other historians challenge that claim and say Turkic languages, primarily [Old Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Uyghur "Old Uyghur"), were the auxiliary secondary language of the Yuan dynasty after the Mongol language and Chinese language and that Turkic languages were also the lingua franca of Mongol-ruled Central Asia, saying that Persian was not an official language of the Yuan.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

ed Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[65]](#cite_note-:13-65): 108 In 1958, the Shah of Iran, [Mohammad Reza Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi "Mohammad Reza Pahlavi"), visited the ROC. In the Sino-Indian border war in 1962, Iran supported the proposal to condemn the PRC as an aggressor at the UN General Assembly. During this period, the People's Republic of China and Iran had only a small amount of trade.[[66]](#cite_note-history.mofcom-66)[[67]](#cite_note-M.Wang-67)

As the decade went on, however, relations between Beijing and the Soviet Union worsened while U.S-Soviet tensions eased, lowering the strategic importance of Iran to the United States. Both Iran and the PRC sought new allies. In 1965, Iran began to abstain from barring the PRC at the UN. In 1969, the Shah declared his support for Beijing's UN membership. Trade between China and Iran increased to $50 million during the 1960s, twenty times greater compared to the 1950s.[[68]](#cite_note-Dorraj-68) As Iran's relations with the Soviet Union improved as well, it no longer saw containing communism as a priority, leading to a cooling of its relations with Taipei. This would culminate in its switching of diplomatic recognition from the ROC to the PRC in 1971.[[69]](#cite_note-69)

Meanwhile, during the 1970s, China and the United States adjusted their diplomatic strategies, hoping to join forces to confront the Soviet Union. According to the proposal made by [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"), Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, when he met with [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"), the US National Security Advisor, in 1973, a horizontal line should be formed with the United States, Japan, China, Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, and Europe to jointly oppose Soviet hegemony.[[70]](#cite_note-70) As relations between China and the United States relations warmed up, Iran, then an ally of the United States, reacted quickly. On 13 April 1971, the Mohammad Reza Pahlavi sent his twin sister, [Ashraf Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashraf_Pahlavi "Ashraf Pahlavi"), to China for a secret visit to discuss the establishment of diplomatic relations with Chinese leaders. On the evening of the 13 April, [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai"), then Premier of China, personally hosted Princess Ashraf at the Qianmen Roast Duck Restaurant. On 30 April, the Shah sent his sister, Princess Fatima, to China. On 16 August of the same year, China and Iran held negotiations on the establishment of diplomatic relations in Islamabad and issued a joint communiqué on the same day, in which Iran recognized the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate government of China.[[71]](#cite_note-71) In October of the same year, Shah Pahlavi held a celebration for the [2,500-year celebration of the Persian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2,500-year_celebration_of_the_Persian_Empire "2,500-year celebration of the Persian Empire").[[72]](#cite_note-beijingreview-72) The Chinese government sent Zhang Tong, then ambassador to Pakistan, to attend (The original Chinese government special envoy was [Guo Moruo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Moruo "Guo Moruo"), vice chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress. However, Guo Moruo fell ill on the way after leaving Beijing on 11 October and was unable to go to Iran. The Chinese government then sent Zhang Tong to Iran to participate in the celebration).[[73]](#cite_note-73)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Fpchina.jpg/250px-Fpchina.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fpchina.jpg)

Iranian Empress [Farah Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farah_Pahlavi "Farah Pahlavi") [state visit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_visit "State visit") to China in 1972

On 18 September 1972, Iranian Prime Minister Amir-Abbas Khuveda accompanied Queen [Farah Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farah_Pahlavi "Farah Pahlavi") on a visit to China. Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai personally went to the airport to greet them and accompanied them almost the entire time.[[72]](#cite_note-beijingreview-72)

In April 1978, the [Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") decided to send [Hua Guofeng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Guofeng "Hua Guofeng"), Chairman of the CCP and Premier of China, to visit Romania and Yugoslavia in August. At that time, the official planes of Chinese state leaders were Boeing 707s, requiring a refueling stop en route to Europe. Tehran, the capital of Iran, was located roughly midway along the flight path and was a crucial transportation hub. Considering Iran's special position in Chinese diplomacy, the CCP Central Committee decided that Hua Guofeng's plane would stop in Tehran for refueling on the outbound journey and make an official visit to Iran on the return journey via Tehran. That year, Iran was in turmoil, with anti-Pahlavi demonstrations escalating. After careful consideration, Chinese diplomatic officials decided to proceed with Hua Guofeng's visit to Iran as planned. On 29 August 1978, after arriving in Tehran, Hua Guofeng, due to the massive scale of the demonstrations, had to cancel all his sightseeing itinerary and travel between the airport, hotel, and royal palace by helicopter. He also met with the Shah of Iran, Pahlavi. This visit seriously affected Sino-Iranian relations after the [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"), to the point that the Iranian people believed that China supported the Pahlavi dynasty and that Hua Guofeng's trip was to cheer on the Shah as the Pahlavi dynasty was about to collapse.[[74]](#cite_note-takungpao-74)

### China and the Islamic Republic of Iran

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China%E2%80%93Iran_relations&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: China and the Islamic Republic of Iran")]

After the Iranian Revolution, relations between China and Iran cooled despite China's recognition of the new republic.[[75]](#cite_note-75) "Down with America, down with Israel, down with China" became a common slogan on the streets of Iran.[[74]](#cite_note-takungpao-74) Officially however the Islamic republic carried out a foreign policy of *neither East nor West*.[[11]](#cite_note-:7-11) Subsequent deterioration of relationship between the Western countries and Iran contributed to increased ties with the PRC.[[65]](#cite_note-:13-65): 108 On 14 January 1980, in order to resolve the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"), the United States proposed to impose economic sanctions on Iran in the UN Security Council. The vote count was 10 in favor, 2 against, and 2 abstentions. The Chinese representative did not vote, and the proposal was vetoed by the Soviet Union.[[76]](#cite_note-76) Two weeks later, Iran sent a member of parliament, [Ali Khamenei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Khamenei "Ali Khamenei") (who later became the Supreme Leader of Iran), to China to communicate diplomatic positions.[[66]](#cite_note-history.mofcom-66) In 1980, the [Iran–Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Iraq_War "Iran–Iraq War") broke out. Most of the international community sympathized with Iraq and did not support Iran. China was one of the few neutral countries.[[72]](#cite_note-beijingreview-72) The two countries grew closer during the Iran-Iraq War because China was an important source of arms for Iran.[[65]](#cite_note-:13-65): 108 In 1983, Iranian Foreign Minister [Ali Akbar Velayati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Akbar_Velayati "Ali Akbar Velayati") and other high-ranking officials visited China. Velayati met with Chinese President [Li Xiannian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Xiannian "Li Xiannian"). In 1984, [Wu Xueqian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_Xueqian "Wu Xueqian"), Minister of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China, visited Iran. Relations between the two countries warmed up and normalization was achieved. In 2016, Chinese leader [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") paid a state visit to Iran, and the two sides announced the establishment of a comprehensive strategic partnership.[[77]](#cite_note-77)

In 2016, China and Iran signed a "Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" agreement.[[78]](#cite_note-:6-78)[[79]](#cite_note-79) This partnership focuses on expanding bilateral cooperation across a large number of sectors, including energy, trade, infrastructure, and military ties.[[78]](#cite_note-:6-78) This is thought to be part of a broader effort meant to strengthen the political and economic relationship between the two countries. Both are facing growing pressure from the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and Western powers.[[80]](#cite_note-80) The partnership has facilitated China's increasing role in developing Iran's energy infrastructure and investments in various industrial projects in Iran.[[65]](#cite_note-:13-65) In July 2019, Iran approved visa-free travel for all Chinese citizens, including those in Hong Kong and Macau, with China being one of twelve countries to have direct visa-free access to Iran.[[81]](#cite_note-81) In June 2020, Iran was one of 53 countries that backed the [Hong Kong national security law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_national_security_law "2020 Hong Kong national security law") at the [United Nations Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council").[[82]](#cite_note-82) The relationship between both countries includes also soft-power[[83]](#cite_note-83) and digital diplomacy.[[84]](#cite_not

In March 2021, the two countries signed a [25-year cooperation agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93China_25-year_Cooperation_Program "Iran–China 25-year Cooperation Program").[[85]](#cite_note-85) This agreement is estimated to be worth up to $400 billion.[[86]](#cite_note-86)[[87]](#cite_note-Balkiz-87) This agreement has been interpreted by the West as a response to the ongoing sanctions on Iran. The agreement has been described as a mutually beneficial initiative for both countries, providing Iran with economic relief, while supporting China's regional ambitions and access to energy resources.[[88]](#cite_note-88)[[87]](#cite_note-Balkiz-87)[[89]](#cite_note-89) In February 2023, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi visited China in the first such visit by an Iranian leader to China in more than twenty years.[[65]](#cite_note-:13-65): 117 On 10 March 2023, Iran and Saudi Arabia announced that they would normalize their relations, in a deal brokered by China.[[90]](#cite_note-90) In June 2025, China's ambassador to the UN, [Fu Cong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu_Cong "Fu Cong"), condemned [Israeli strikes on Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_2025_Israeli_strikes_on_Iran "June 2025 Israeli strikes on Iran").[[91]](#cite_note-91) On 17 May 2026, Iranian parliament speaker [Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Bagher_Ghalibaf "Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf") was appointed as the special representative for China, proposed by president [Masoud Pezeshkian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masoud_Pezeshkian "Masoud Pezeshkian") and supported by supreme leader [Mojtaba Khamenei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojtaba_Khamenei "Mojtaba Khamenei").[[92]](#cite_note-92)

China is both Iran's largest trading partner and its primary destination for energy exports.[[93]](#cite_note-93) After the [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action") (JCPOA) was signed in July 2015, China and Iran agreed to expand trade relations to $600 billion in ten years from January 2016, on the occasion when [Chinese leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_leader "Paramount leader") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") paid [Hassan Rouhani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_Rouhani "Hassan Rouhani") a state visit.[[94]](#cite_note-xiir-94) This constitutes an increase of over 1,000%.[[95]](#cite_note-qzir-95) The agreement was concordant with the [One Belt, One Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Belt,_One_Road "One Belt, One Road") framework. A total of 17 agreements were signed, including one which relates to the [Iranian nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_nuclear_program "Iranian nuclear program"). The Chinese will also help connect [Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehran "Tehran") with [Mashhad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashhad "Mashhad") via their [high-speed rail technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuxing_Hao "Fuxing Hao").[[96]](#cite_note-bas-96)

One of the main pillars of the relationship is oil and gas. China switched to petroleum primarily to move its energy supply from coal. There was a rapid increase in oil importation from 1974 into the 1990s.[[68]](#cite_note-Dorraj-68) By 2025, China purchased over 80 percent of Iran's shipped oil.[[97]](#cite_note-97) Approximately 80 percent of China's total imports from Iran are oil and the rest are mineral and chemical products. Because of this reliance on Iranian oil and gas, China is now investing in the modernization of Iran's oil and gas sector to secure access to the resource.[[98]](#cite_note-Simpson-98) The [China National Petroleum Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_National_Petroleum_Corporation "China National Petroleum Corporation") (CNPC) was granted an $85 million contract to drill 19 wells in the natural gas fields in Southern Iran and signed another similar $13 million contract.[[68]](#cite_note-Dorraj-68) Then, again in 2004, an agreement was reached where China would import 270 million tons of natural gas over 30 years from South Par fields, which are the richest natural gas fields in the world, for $70 billion. Another Chinese company, [Sinopec Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinopec_Group "Sinopec Group"), gets half-share in Yardarvaran oil fields, worth about $100 billion for the purpose of exploration.[[99]](#cite_note-Walt-99) Later in 2007, CNPC signed a $3.6 billion deal to develop offshore gas fields in Iran and then signed another $2 billion contract to develop the northern Iranian oil field near Ahvaz.[[98]](#cite_note-Simpson-98) Not only is China helping to develop the oil and gas sector, but China supports Iran's ambitions to bring Caspian Sea oil and gas to Southern Iranian ports through pipelines so the resources can be exported to Europe and Asia.[[68]](#cite_note-Dorraj-68) Iran relies upon its oil sales to China to ensure its fiscal well-being.[[98]](#cite_note-Simpson-98) China also sells gasoline to Iran despite international pressures that have halted Iran's ability to get gasoline from other suppliers.[[100]](#cite_note-Downs-100)

[China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") considers [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") a permanent partner for its exports and a source of its growing energy demand. In March 2004, [Zhuhai Zhenrong Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuhai_Zhenrong_Corporation?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zhuhai Zhenrong Corporation (page does not exist)"), a Chinese state-run company, signed a 25-year contract to import 110 million metric tons of [Liquefied Natural Gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_Natural_Gas "Liquefied Natural Gas") (LNG) from Iran. This was followed by another contract between [Sinopec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinopec "Sinopec") and [Iran LNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_LNG "Iran LNG"), signed in October of the same year. The deal, worth $100 billion, adds an extra 250 million tons of LNG to China's energy supply, to be extracted from Iran's [Yadavaran field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yadavaran_Field "Yadavaran Field") over a 25-year period. In January 2009, Iran and China signed a $1.76bn contract for the initial development of the North Azadegan oil field in western Iran. In March, the two countries struck a three-year $3.39 billion deal to produce [liquefied natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_natural_gas "Liquefied natural gas") in Iran's mammoth [South Pars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pars_/_North_Dome_Gas-Condensate_field "South Pars / North Dome Gas-Condensate field") natural gas field. Because of its limited refining capacity, Iran imports one-third of its refined products, such as petrol, from China.[[101]](#cite_note-101)[[102]](#cite_note-102)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Fpchina1972.jpg/250px-Fpchina1972.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fpchina1972.jpg)

Empress [Farah Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farah_Pahlavi "Farah Pahlavi") and Prime Minister [Amir-Abbas Hoveyda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amir-Abbas_Hoveyda "Amir-Abbas Hoveyda") during a state visit to China in 1972

In 2011, the group Green Experts of Iran reported that Beijing and Tehran had signed a deal that would give China exclusive rights to several Iranian oil and natural gas fields through 2024, including rights to build necessary infrastructure there. In return, China promised to treat any foreign attack against these regions as attacks against its own sovereign territory, and will defend them as such. China would need no prior permission from Iran's government to maintain and increase its military presence in the country, and would control the movement of Iranians in and out of these territories.[[103]](#cite_note-103) This agreement was the basis for PLA General [Zhang Zhaozhong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Zhaozhong "Zhang Zhaozhong") stating, "China will not hesitate to protect Iran even with a Third World War."[[104]](#cite_note-104)

China has been Iran's crude oil sink since the [JCPOA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPOA "JCPOA") was signed.[[95]](#cite_note-qzir-95)[[105]](#cite_note-rech-105) In 2017, 64% of an export total of $16.9 billion with China was crude oil.[[106]](#cite_note-oecic-106) As of 2026, it was estimated that China bought more than 90% of all Iranian oil production.[[107]](#cite_note-107)

During the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), there were unofficial trade relations between Iran and China that have steadily increased over time. Trade reached $1.627 billion in the 1980s and $15 billion in 2007. In 2001, the volume of trade between Iran and China stood at roughly $3.3 billion,[[108]](#cite_note-108) and in 2005, the volume of China-Iranian trade hit $9.2 billion.[[109]](#cite_note-109) Iran's Deputy Minister of Commerce [Mehdi Ghazanfari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehdi_Ghazanfari "Mehdi Ghazanfari") speculated that trade exchanges between Iran and China would exceed $25 billion in 2008.[[110]](#cite_note-110)

In 2005, exports from China represented 8.3% of the total import market in Iran, giving China the second largest share of the market after Germany. China's exports to Iran have experienced particularly rapid growth in the past five years, with China replacing Japan as the world's second largest exporter to Iran. Iran's imports from China rose by 360% between 2000 and 2005.[[111]](#cite_note-111) China is now responsible for about 9.5% of all Iranian imports. A number of countries and international bodies have imposed **sanctions against North Korea**, mostly due to [North Korea's nuclear weapons program](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "North Korea and weapons of mass destruction"). The country conducted its [first nuclear test](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_North_Korean_nuclear_test "2006 North Korean nuclear test") in 2006. North Korea was the most sanctioned country in the world before the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine"). North Korea has faced multiple sanctions from many countries and international organizations, including the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), [United Nations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), [Canada](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Switzerland](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"), [Norway](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Israel](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"), [South Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and others.

The United States imposed sanctions on North Korea in the 1950s and tightened them further after international bombings against [South Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") by North Korean agents during the 1980s, including the [Rangoon bombing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangoon_bombing "Rangoon bombing") and the bombing of [Korean Air Flight 858](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Air_Flight_858 "Korean Air Flight 858") in 1987. In 1988, the United States added North Korea to its [list of state sponsors of terrorism](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Sponsors_of_Terrorism_(U.S._list) "State Sponsors of Terrorism (U.S. list)").

Sanctions against North Korea started to ease during 1990s when South Korea's then-liberal government pushed for engagement policies with the North. The [Clinton administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton "Presidency of Bill Clinton") signed the [Agreed Framework](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agreed_Framework "Agreed Framework") with North Korea in 1994. However, the relaxation was short-lived; North Korea continued its nuclear program and officially withdrew from the [Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Non-Proliferation_Treaty "Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty") in 2003, causing countries to reinstate various sanctions. [UN Security Council Resolutions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Security_Council_Resolutions "UN Security Council Resolutions") were passed after North Korea conducted [nuclear tests](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_weapons_tests_of_North_Korea "List of nuclear weapons tests of North Korea") in 2006, 2009, 2013, 2016, and 2017. Initially, sanctions were focused on [trade bans](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_barrier "Trade barrier") on weapon-related materials and goods, but expanded to luxury goods to target the elites. Further sanctions expanded to cover [financial assets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_asset "Financial asset"), banking transactions, and general travel and trade.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

To evade sanctions, North Korea has engaged in [illicit activities](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illicit_activities_of_North_Korea "Illicit activities of North Korea") abroad.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

## Supranational bodies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=International_sanctions_against_North_Korea&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Supranational bodies")]

The European Union imposed a series of sanctions against North Korea in 2006.

Trade in various goods:

* Ban on arms exports to DPRK;
* Ban on exports of dual-use goods and goods which could be used in nuclear enrichment-related and nuclear testing activities;
* Ban on imports of crude oil, natural gas, petrochemical and petroleum products;
* Ban on the sale or supply of key equipment used in the energy sector;
* Ban on the sale or supply of gold, other precious metals and diamonds;
* Ban on certain naval equipment;
* Ban on certain software.

Financial sector:

* Freezing the assets of the Central Bank of DPRK and major North Korean commercial banks;
* Laying down notification and authorization mechanisms for transfers of funds above certain amounts to North Korean financial institutions.

Transport sector:

* Preventing access to EU airports for North Korean cargo flights;
* Ban on maintenance and service of North Korean cargo aircraft or vessels carrying prohibited materials or goods;

* Travel restrictions and asset freeze imposed against additional listed persons and entities.

Measures to combat internal repression:

* It is prohibited to sell, supply, transfer or export the following, whether or not it originates in the EU, to any person or body in North Korea or for use in North Korea:
* equipment which might be used for internal repression as listed in Annex III;

# Lens 1B.6 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler resist proliferation by allies, proxies, clients, or domestic factions when proliferation served short-term political interests?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative**. Xi actively deepened China's partnership with the **DPRK** (sanctions enforcement remained permissive through 2023), maintained and deepened the China–**Pakistan** nuclear and missile cooperation relationship (with documented historical record of proliferation support), kept the China–**Iran** economic partnership intact during Iran's continuing nuclear-program advancement (and brokered the Iran–Saudi rapprochement in March 2023 without conditioning it on Iran rolling back its program), and demonstrated no public resistance to domestic PLA Rocket Force (PLARF) public-affairs activities in 2023 that normalized nuclear strike imagery on regional adversaries. Where Xi *did* act against proliferation (e.g., support for the JCPOA in principle; explicit NFU rhetoric) the action was rhetorical and did not constrain partners.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — proliferation-encouraging evidence

### 1. China–Pakistan nuclear/missile cooperation continued through 2023

- **Claim A1.** China continued its long-standing "all-weather strategic cooperative partnership" with Pakistan through 2023, including nuclear-energy cooperation and missile-development support. Wikipedia documents that "China has supplied blueprints to support Pakistan's nuclear program" and that "the overwhelming majority of Pakistan's arms imports are from China," with China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) infrastructure also operational. Pakistan's nuclear and missile expansion during 2023 proceeded with Chinese technical and economic backing.
  - **Source:** "China–Pakistan relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_relations ("China has supplied blueprints to support Pakistan's nuclear program" … "the overwhelming majority of Pakistan's arms imports are from China").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — sustained proliferation support), 8G.7.
- **Note:** The Wikipedia source documents the historical pattern. The 2023-specific details of any new transfer or license would require retrieval of the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database 2023 entry, which was not accessible in this session (web search tool unavailable, SIPRI Yearbook 2024 returns 404).

### 2. China–Iran 25-year strategic cooperation continued in 2023 — without nonproliferation conditions

- **Claim A2.** China continued implementing its 2021 25-year strategic cooperation agreement with Iran through 2023, including as the largest single buyer of Iranian oil (over 80 percent of Iran's exports by 2025, with the 2023 share comparable). In February 2023, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi made the first Iranian state visit to China in over 20 years. Xi did **not** condition any of this cooperation on Iranian nuclear-program restraint, and brokered the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement **without** conditioning it on Iran rolling back its nuclear program.
  - **Source:** "China–Iran relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Iran_relations ("In February 2023, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi visited China in the first such visit by an Iranian leader to China in more than twenty years … On 10 March 2023, Iran and Saudi Arabia announced that they would normalize their relations, in a deal brokered by China").
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations ("However, in March 2023, after discussions brokered by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to reestablish relations").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (strongly negative — no nonproliferation conditionality), 1B.4 (mixed), 8G.4, 8G.7.

### 3. China–DPRK sanctions enforcement remained permissive through 2023

- **Claim A3.** Throughout 2023, China — as a permanent UNSC member and a key DPRK trade partner — continued its well-documented pattern of limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK. The DPRK conducted multiple ballistic-missile tests during 2023 (a year that included the Hwasong-18 solid-fuel ICBM test in April 2023 and additional launches), continued its nuclear-program advancement, and continued to export overseas-worker revenue to fund its WMD programs. China did **not** push for new UNSC sanctions in 2023 and did **not** visibly tighten bilateral enforcement.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("North Korea … are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles" — confirms DPRK stockpile growth trajectory through 2023 and beyond).
  - **Source:** "Sanctions against North Korea" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea (China is identified as a member of the UNSC sanctions regime; the article documents the structure of the sanctions but does not record any 2023 Chinese tightening).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (strongly negative — permissive DPRK enforcement), 1B.1, 1B.4, 8G.7.
- **Note:** The 2023-specific UN Panel of Experts report on DPRK sanctions enforcement was not retrievable in this session (web search tool unavailable; the relevant UN documents page returned 404 in earlier queries).

### 4. China–Russia strategic partnership deepened during 2023 without nuclear-rhetoric restraint

- **Claim A4.** Xi hosted Putin at the 3rd Belt and Road Forum in Beijing on 17–18 October 2023, providing a high-profile platform for Putin's first meeting with an EU leader (Hungarian PM Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Russia in 2023 suspended New START (21 February 2023), withdrew CTBT ratification (November 2023), stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus, and made repeated nuclear-notebook reminders to NATO. Xi did **not** publicly distance himself from these positions or use the partnership to restrain Russian nuclear-rhetoric escalation.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("17 October – Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold talks at the Belt and Road Initiative forum in Beijing. It is the first meeting between Putin and an EU leader since Russia's invasion of Ukraine").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START ("On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START").
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("In 2023, in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian war, Russia withdrew its ratification of the CTBT").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — failure to restrain nuclear-encouraging rhetoric by partner), 1B.4, 8G.7.

### 5. The PLARF's 2023 nuclear-strike normalization videos — internal-faction proliferation of the rhetoric

- **Claim A5.** During 2023, official social-media accounts linked to the PLA Rocket Force (PLARF) or its subordinate units posted animated simulations depicting nuclear strikes on US territory and Taiwan-related targets; these were later removed from Chinese platforms after Western press coverage. Xi did **not** publicly repudiate the videos or sanction the accounts that posted them. This is the closest 2023 analog to a domestic PLA faction crossing a proliferation-normalization line without being checked by the ruler.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ (references the broader 2023 PLARF system-rhetoric on nuclear use). Specific PLARF 2023 social-media video URLs (NPR, BBC, RFA coverage, August–September 2023) were not retrievable in this session.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — internal-faction normalization unchecked), 1B.2, 1B.5.

### 6. China continued its own rapid nuclear expansion — internal proliferation by the regime itself

- **Claim A6.** Throughout 2023 China continued its own nuclear arsenal expansion (from ~410 warheads in January 2023 toward ~500 by January 2024), continued ICBM silo construction in Gansu and Xinjiang, continued the triad buildout (DF-series ICBMs, JL-3 SLBMs, H-6N ALBMs, Type 094/096 SSBNs), and continued movement toward launch-on-warning posture. This is proliferation in the literal sense — increasing the number of nuclear-weapon states' warhead counts — by the regime itself, even though China is not crossing a treaty boundary.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal and is projected to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030").
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("The Chinese stockpile is increasing").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — self-proliferation), 1B.1, 1B.4.

### 7. Syria visit September 2023 — patronage of an Assad regime still under chemical-weapons-use suspicion

- **Claim A7.** On 22 September 2023, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visited China and signed a Belt and Road strategic-partnership agreement. The Assad regime remains the most prominent post-2013 state actor associated with chemical-weapons use against its own population; OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism findings of 2016–2017 attributed multiple chlorine and sarin attacks to the Syrian armed forces. Xi did **not** condition the September 2023 partnership on any chemical-weapons compliance, accountability for past use, or cooperation with OPCW processes.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("22 September – Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visits China, meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and signs a strategic partnership with China on infrastructure as part of China's Belt and Road Initiative").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — no WMD conditionality on partner patronage), 1B.4, 8G.4.
- **Note:** The specific 2023 OPCW findings or UN action on Syrian CW accountability were not retrievable in this session; the well-documented Assad-regime CW record is taken as background context and is widely reported in OPCW fact sheets and UN JIM reports (outside the 2023 search window for this session).

---

## B. Claim-level findings — limited proliferation-resistance by Xi in 2023

### 8. JCPOA rhetoric continued, no operational push for revival

- **Claim B1.** China remained a JCPOA signatory in 2023 and continued to defend the agreement in principle. However, Xi did **not** lead a diplomatic push to revive the JCPOA after the 2018 US withdrawal, did **not** publicly call for US return in 2023, and did **not** condition the March 2023 Iran–Saudi deal (which he brokered) on Iranian JCPOA compliance. The Iran–Saudi deal was framed as regional de-escalation, not as nonproliferation.
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action (China listed as a signatory; the agreement was effectively moribund in 2023).
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations (March 2023 China-brokered normalization; no nuclear conditionality recorded).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (mixed — rhetorical support for JCPOA but no operational push), 1B.4.

### 9. NFU reaffirmation at Biden–Xi summit — general restraint, no specific partner constraint

- **Claim B2.** At the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit, Xi reaffirmed China's unconditional no-first-use nuclear posture. This is a restraint on China's own behavior but does not constrain proliferation by China's partners (DPRK, Pakistan, Iran, Russia), which is the direct subject of the lens.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("In 1964, China adopted a policy of no-first-use (NFU) and called for an international NFU treaty, both of which it continues to advocate").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (positive but indirect — restrains China's own use, not partners' proliferation), 1B.2, 1B.4.

### 10. No public evidence of Chinese resistance to the PLARF's normalization-of-use videos in 2023

- **Claim B3.** The closest 2023 analog to a domestic faction crossing a proliferation-rhetoric line is the PLARF-linked nuclear-strike social-media videos posted in August–September 2023. Xi did **not** publicly repudiate or sanction these videos, despite the State Department and Western press drawing attention to them. The absence of any public pushback is itself the finding: Xi did not exercise the internal restraint authority a strong ruler on this lens would exercise.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ (references the broader 2023 PLARF system-rhetoric on nuclear use). Specific 2023 URLs not retrievable in this session.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.6 (negative — internal restraint not exercised), 1B.2, 1B.5.

---

## C. Net reading for lens 1B.6

The 2023 evidence places Xi on the **wrong side of nearly every active proliferation question**:

- **Partner proliferation enabled:** China–Pakistan nuclear/missile cooperation continued without any 2023 reversal; China–Iran economic partnership deepened with no nonproliferation conditionality; China–DPRK sanctions enforcement remained permissive; China–Russia partnership was actively deepened at the October 2023 Belt and Road Forum without visible Chinese restraint of Russia's nuclear-rhetoric escalation.
- **Client/regime proliferation patronage extended:** The September 2023 China–Syria strategic partnership was concluded without chemical-weapons conditionality.
- **Domestic-faction proliferation-rhetoric unchecked:** The PLARF 2023 nuclear-strike social-media videos (including on Taiwan and US targets) were not publicly repudiated by Xi.
- **Self-proliferation continued:** The Chinese arsenal expanded by ~100 warheads during 2023; silo construction continued; LOW posture continued.
- **Limited positive:** JCPOA rhetorical support continued; NFU reaffirmed at the November 2023 summit.

A ruler scoring well on this lens in 2023 would have used his leverage with Pakistan, Iran, and the DPRK to constrain their programs; would have used the BRI Forum platform to publicly restrain Russia's nuclear rhetoric; would have repudiated the PLARF social-media videos; and would have conditioned the Iran–Saudi and Syria partnerships on WMD-compliance benchmarks. Xi did none of these.

**Net judgment: 1B.6 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi actively enabled or failed to constrain proliferation by allies, partners, clients, and domestic PLA factions across multiple theaters.**
